item.title: Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes
item.description:
Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes

Goose is a database migration tool available as both a CLI and a library. It allows developers to manage database schemas by creating incremental SQL changes or Go functions.

🔍 Overview

The tool supports migrations for multiple database systems. It works against Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Spanner, SQLite, YDB, ClickHouse, MSSQL, and Vertica.

🧩 How it works

Goose supports specific migration formats and operational features:

  • Go migrations written as plain functions.
  • Embedded migrations.
  • Out-of-order migrations.
  • Seeding data.
  • Environment variable substitution in SQL migrations.

⚙️ Key details

The CLI includes flags for configuring migration behavior. The following table details specific flags and their functions:

Flag Description
-allow-missing Applies missing (out-of-order) migrations
-certfile File path to root CA’s certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-dir Directory with migration files (default “.”, can be set via GOOSE_MIGRATION_DIR)
-env Load environment variables from file (default .env)
-no-color Disable color output (NO_COLOR env variable supported)
-no-versioning Apply migration commands with no versioning, in file order
-s Use sequential numbering for new migrations
-ssl-cert File path to SSL certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-ssl-key File path to SSL key in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-table Migrations table name (default “goose_db_version”)
-timeout Maximum allowed duration for queries to run

🚀 Availability

Goose is available via several installation methods:

  • Go Install: go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest installs the binary to your $GOPATH/bin directory.
  • Homebrew: Available for macOS users.
  • Docker: A container image is available for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
    • The container image has no shell and supports .sql migrations only.
    • The working directory is /migrations.
    • Tags include vX.Y.Z, vX.Y, vX, and latest.
    • Dockerfiles can copy the binary using: COPY --from=ghcr.io/pressly/goose:v3.30.1 /usr/local/bin/goose /usr/local/bin/goose

#Goose #Database #Go #CLI #Migrations

Source: pressly/goose

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 reaches GA and is available on Lakebase
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 reaches GA and is available on Lakebase

PostgreSQL 19 reached general availability today and is already available on Lakebase. Several engineers on the Lakebase team are PostgreSQL committers and contributors who worked on this release directly, from query plan advice to shared memory, locale handling, and release management. New major versions often take weeks to reach other managed PostgreSQL services.

🔍 Overview

PostgreSQL 19 is a practical release with no single headline feature that changes what PostgreSQL is. Instead, version 19 goes after operational problems that database teams know well:

  • Bloated tables
  • Unstable query plans
  • Replica lag
  • Incomplete statistics
  • Maintenance work that is hard to run safely in production

🧩 Key Features

  • REPACK — reclaims space while normal reads and writes continue during most of the operation
  • pg_plan_advice — describes planner decisions as advice, applies supplied advice, and reports whether it was followed
  • pg_stash_advice — stores advice by query ID and applies it automatically when a matching query is planned

⚙️ How REPACK Works

PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control, so an UPDATE creates a new row version and a DELETE leaves a dead tuple behind. Routine vacuuming makes that space reusable, but it doesn’t necessarily return space to the operating system or restore a useful physical row order. The usual fixes — VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, or external tools such as pg_repack — take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole operation, blocking normal access to the table.

REPACK reclaims space like VACUUM FULL; with USING INDEX, it also physically orders rows like CLUSTER. With CONCURRENTLY, PostgreSQL rebuilds the table while normal reads and writes continue, capturing ongoing changes through logical decoding. It then takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to apply any remaining captured changes and swap the new table and index files into place.

Component Role
pg_plan_advice Describes planner decisions as advice, applies supplied advice, reports whether it was followed
pg_stash_advice Stores advice by query ID and applies it automatically when a matching query is planned

These components do not add cross-table statistics or replace the planner. Instead, they let you intervene when an inaccurate estimate produces a poor plan. Unlike inline optimizer hints, plan advice lives outside the application’s query text. You can inspect the current plan, test focused advice, and then stash it by query ID.

⚠️ REPACK Limitations

Concurrent repacking creates an additional replication slot for the duration of the operation, so it needs free capacity under max_repack_replication_slots and a table with either a non-deferrable primary key or a suitable index-based replica identity. It also needs temporary disk space for a copy of the table and all its indexes, potentially plus a sort file up to the size of the table.

Tables with heavy update and delete traffic face an additional limit: the current upstream PostgreSQL 19 implementation fails if more than about 104 million tuples in the target table are updated or deleted while REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) is running. This counts changes made during the repack, not rows already in the table.

Concurrent repacking is also not MVCC-safe: after it commits, transactions using snapshots taken before the repack began can see the table as empty. Physical clustering also degrades as later writes arrive. REPACK CONCURRENTLY still needs planning, but it brings into core a job that previously required more downtime or an extension.

🚀 Availability

To try it, create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19 as the version.

#PostgreSQL #Lakebase #Database #GARelease #REPACK #QueryPlanning

Source: PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19 Released with New Read-Your-Writes Consistency Feature

PostgreSQL 19 has been released, arriving two months later than the typical September schedule due to a flurry of issues related to AI-reported vulnerabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • The release was delayed from September by two months.
  • The delay was attributed to addressing ongoing AI-reported vulnerability issues.
  • The author considers the release “definitely worth the wait.”

🧩 How it works

The release introduces a “read-your-writes” consistency feature for applications sending reads to standbys using the new WAIT FOR LSN command. This allows a session on a standby to wait until it has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query. This ensures the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

Example Workflow

  1. Update a record on the primary: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
  2. Get the current LSN: SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); (returns a value like 0/0306EE20).
  3. Store the LSN value (e.g., in a signed cookie).
  4. On a subsequent request, use the stored LSN on a standby: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
  5. Run the query: SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout parameter is optional. If provided, the system returns an error if the replica does not catch up within the specified time.

💡 Why it matters

This pattern ensures users see events in chronological order and maintain a consistent view across subsequent requests. Similar patterns have previously been implemented in hand-rolled solutions:

  • Wikipedia/MediaWiki: Uses a hand-rolled version against MySQL replication, saving the primary binlog position in the session and waiting for replicas to catch up before reads. MediaWiki now uses MySQL’s WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

#PostgreSQL #Database #SQL #DataConsistency #WaitForLSN

Source: PostgreSQL 19 Released

item.title: Milvus Backup: Command-Line Tool for Milvus Data Management
item.description:
Milvus Backup: Command-Line Tool for Milvus Data Management

Milvus Backup is a command-line tool and API service for backing up and restoring Milvus data. It allows backup and restore operations to run while the Milvus cluster remains available.

🔍 Overview

  • Milvus Backup is a command-line tool and API service for backing up and restoring Milvus data.
  • Backup and restore operations run while the Milvus cluster remains available.

⚙️ Key details

  • Download a binary from the release page, or install it with Homebrew on macOS:
    • brew install zilliztech/tap/milvus-backup
  • To build from source instead, run make all; the executable is written to ./milvus-backup.
  • Milvus Backup reads its connection settings from a configuration file.
  • Copy the example and update it for your deployment — Configuration explains what to change:
    • cp configs/backup.yaml backup.yaml
  • Then validate the setup and run your first backup and restore:
    • milvus-backup check
    • milvus-backup create -n my_backup
    • milvus-backup list
    • milvus-backup restore -n my_backup

🚀 Availability

  • The latest version supports backups from Milvus 2.2 and later, and restores to Milvus 2.5 and later.
  • A backup can be restored only to the same or a newer Milvus version.

💡 Why it matters

  • Milvus Backup allows for the management of Milvus data with ease, ensuring data availability and integrity.
  • It supports various commands for different operations, making it a versatile tool for Milvus data management.

#Milvus #Backup #DataManagement #AI #Database

Source: zilliztech/milvus-backup

item.title: LanceDB Provides Open Source and Enterprise Vector Search Options
item.description:
LanceDB Provides Open Source and Enterprise Vector Search Options

LanceDB has launched as a database designed for fast, scalable, and production-ready vector search. The system is built on the Lance columnar format, serving as a central location for developers to build, train, and analyze AI workloads while storing and indexing petabytes of multimodal data.

🔍 Overview

LanceDB supports comprehensive search capabilities, including vector similarity search, full-text search, and SQL. It allows users to store, query, and filter vectors, metadata, and multimodal data such as text, images, videos, and point clouds. The platform is engineered to search billions of vectors in milliseconds using state-of-the-art indexing.

🧩 How it works

The database is built on the Lance columnar format, which provides efficient storage and analytics. Advanced features include zero-copy operations and automatic versioning, allowing users to manage data versions without requiring extra infrastructure. The system also supports GPU usage in the process of building vector indexes.

⚙️ Key details

LanceDB is available in two primary configurations:

Version Description
LanceDB Embedded (open source) Runs in the application’s process; data resides on local disk or in object storage; 100% open source with no vendor lock-in.
LanceDB Enterprise Offers production-scale distributed search, indexing, and maintenance, plus complete data sovereignty and security.

🚀 Availability

Developers can integrate LanceDB through Python, Node.js, Rust, and REST APIs. Native support is provided for Python and JavaScript/TypeScript, with API and SDK support available for Python, TypeScript, and Rust.

#LanceDB #VectorSearch #Database #MultimodalAI

Source: lancedb/lancedb

item.title: Security Update Resolves Unauthorized Access in Database Registration Routing
item.description:
Security Update Resolves Unauthorized Access in Database Registration Routing

A minor security fix has been backported from version 1.0a43 to address a vulnerability that allowed unauthorized database downloads. This update resolves a security issue occurring when database routes and names do not match.

⚙️ Key details

  • Affected Registration: The issue involves databases registered using add_database(db, name=..., route=...).
  • Vulnerability Condition: The security flaw occurred when a database was registered with a route that differed from its name.
  • Access Restriction Bypass: In these instances, actors who were denied access to the database could still download it from the /<route>.db endpoint.

🚀 Availability

  • The security fix was backported from version 1.0a43.

#Cybersecurity #Database #SoftwarePatch

Source: Release: datasette 0.65.6

item.title: A Decade of Database Innovation: The Amazon Aurora Story
item.description:
🚀 A Decade of Database Innovation: The Amazon Aurora Story

![Amazon Aurora Architecture](https://assets.amazon.science/dims4/default/16f2f5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/220 6x694+0+0/resize/1200x378!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Famazon-topics-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.co m%2Fscience%2Fee%2F98%2Fda80d68b4f2d853d23cacd76e592%2Fscreenshot-2025-08-20-at-12-10-55-pm.png)

Original screenshots of Aurora from Jeff Barr’s blog post

☁️ Introduction: Reimagining Databases for the Cloud Era

When Andy Jassy announced Amazon Aurora in 2014, the promise was revolutionary yet practical: a relational database built specifically for the cloud that would combine MySQL’s cost-effectiveness with the performance of high-end commercial databases. The ambitious goal was five times the throughput of MySQL at one-tenth the price of traditional commercial solutions.

🏗️ The Architecture Revolution: Decoupling Storage from Comput

Aurora’s launch in 2015 marked a fundamental shift in database architecture. Unlike traditional databases where computation and storage are tightly coupled, Aurora decoupled these components, enabling:

  • Independent scaling of computational tasks and storage
  • Automated backups and replication
  • Enhanced reliability without performance sacrifice
  • Easy adaptation to variable workloads

![Aurora Architecture Paper](https://assets.amazon.science/dims4/default/0f3c103/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1402x1246+ 0+0/resize/1200x1066!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Famazon-topics-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fs cience%2F68%2Fab%2F14d45f7840aea08c042889e0b38d%2Fscreenshot-2025-08-20-at-12-17-43-pm.png)

Amazon researchers describe Aurora’s innovative architecture in their 2017 SIGMOD paper

💡 Key Innovation: Moving Beyond Network Constraints

As Werner Vogels, Amazon’s CTO, explained in 2019:

“To start addressing the limitations of relational databases, we reconceptualized the stack by decomposing the system into its fundamental building blocks. We recognized that the caching and logging layers were ripe for innovation.”

The team addressed the central constraint in high-throughput data processing: the network bottleneck. Aurora’s novel service-oriented architecture provided:

  • Independent fault-tolerant storage across multiple data centers
  • Self-healing capabilities
  • Protection from performance variance
  • Resilience against transient or permanent failures

📈 Unprecedented Growth and Adoption

Within just two years, Aurora became the fastest-growing service in AWS history. The diverse customer base included:

  • Financial services companies
  • Gaming companies
  • Healthcare providers
  • Educational institutions
  • Startups of all sizes

🔄 The Serverless Evolution

Aurora Serverless (2018)

The introduction of Aurora Serverless marked another leap forward, providing:

  • On-demand autoscaling configuration
  • Automatic capacity adjustment based on workload
  • Pay-per-use pricing model
  • Elimination of explicit capacity management

![Aurora Serverless Paper](https://assets.amazon.science/dims4/default/0fe5486/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1338x1242+ 0+0/resize/1200x1114!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Famazon-topics-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fs cience%2Fc0%2F29%2Faa542fe14dee9fa07bb7d383f60e%2Fscreenshot-2025-08-20-at-12-21-00-pm.png)

The 2024 VLDB paper describes Aurora Serverless as a fully managed, autoscaling solution

Complete Serverless Transformation (2025)

As of May 2025, all Aurora offerings are now serverless, eliminating the need for customers to worry about:

  • Server type or size selection
  • Underlying hardware management
  • Operating system maintenance
  • Backup management
  • System patching

🎓 Real-World Impact: Arizona State University Case Study

John Rome, Deputy CIO at Arizona State University, exemplifies Aurora’s value proposition:

“We see Amazon Aurora Serverless as a next step in our cloud maturity to help us improve development agility while reducing costs on infrequently used systems.”

ASU’s Challenge: Managing data needs for 73,000+ students across multiple campuses with dramatic seasonal variations.

Aurora’s Solution: Elastic scaling that allows ASU to pay only for resources used while maintaining performance during peak periods.

📊 Measurable Business Value

According to International Data Corporation (IDC) research, organizations using Aurora achieve:

Metric Improvement
3-Year ROI 434%
Operational Cost Reduction 42%
Performance vs. MySQL 5x throughput
Cost vs. Commercial DBs 90% reduction

🔮 Future Innovations on the Horizon

The 2024 research paper outlined several exciting future directions:

  • Predictive live migration techniques
  • Statistical multiplexing for complementary resource needs
  • Advanced ML/RL-based workload prediction
  • Enhanced decision-making algorithms

![AWS Team at re:Invent 2024](https://assets.amazon.science/dims4/default/f4d5553/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x3024+0 +0/resize/1200x900!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Famazon-topics-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fsci ence%2Ffe%2F63%2F7fb0eb7046ab97f2985054d545af%2Fswami-at-kiosk-aurora-10-year-tshirts.jpg)

Swami Sivasubramanian (center), VP of AWS Agentic AI, and the AWS databases team celebrating Aurora’s 10th anniversary at re:Invent 2024

🙌 Credits

Originally posted at: https://www.amazon.science/blog/a-decade-of-database-innovation-the-amazon-aurora-story

✅ Final Thoughts

Aurora’s decade-long journey represents more than just technological evolution—it demonstrates how reimagining fundamental architectural constraints can create transformative solutions. From its initial promise of combining MySQL’s simplicity with enterprise-grade performance to its current fully serverless incarnation, Aurora has consistently pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in cloud-native database technology.

The transition from traditional coupled architectures to Aurora’s decoupled, service-oriented approach has not only delivered on its original performance and cost promises but has also enabled entirely new paradigms like serverless computing. As organizations continue their digital transformation journeys, Aurora’s evolution from a revolutionary idea to an industry-standard solution illustrates the power of customer-obsessed innovation in the cloud era.

Looking ahead, with advances in machine learning, predictive analytics, and automated resource management, Aurora is positioned to continue leading database innovation for the next decade and beyond.

#AWS #AURORA #DATABASE #CLOUDCOMPUTING #SERVERLESS #MYSQL #POSTGRESQL #INNOVATION #MACHINELEARNING
